newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Brash hopes NZ bank disclosure will spur debate.
newsitem.headline: Brash hopes NZ bank disclosure will spur debate.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said on Friday he was confident that the country's new bank disclosure regime was playing an important role in strengthening market disciplines on banks.
New Zealand introduced new supervision arrangements in 1996 which require detailed quarterly public disclosure statements by banks and reduce the extent of central bank prudential regulation.

"We are confident that the disclosure arrangements are playing an important role in strengthening market disciplines on banks. Under the new arrangements, the market has considerably greater information on a bank's financial performance and risk positions than was previously the case," Brash said.
A copy of his address to the International Monetary Fund's conference on banking soundness and monetary policy in Washington was made available in Wellington.
Brash said the market had greater scope under the new system to reward well-managed banks and penalise the less well-managed.
"The strongest banks are likely to benefit from that strength by operating at lower costs; weaker banks are likely to be under pressure to strengthen their position," he said.
The new framework placed greater importance on the role of bank directors. It was likely to increase their accountability and, over time, improve the quality of bank boards.
Brash noted that each of a bank's directors must sign its disclosure statements, and is liable to criminal and civil penalties if these are held to be false or misleading.

Another hoped-for benefit from the disclosure regime was a reduction in the risk that taxpayers would be called upon to rescue a bank. The public now had access to much the same information on banks as did the Reserve Bank, Brash said.
He stressed that the central bank had not abandoned its responsibilities for the financial system.

It saw value in retaining some control, through its registration system, over which entities could call themselves banks; in maintaining a sound understanding of the state of the financial system; and in retaining a capacity to respond to financial distress or bank failure, where this threatened to
"I very much hope that the approach which we in New Zealand have adopted will assist in promoting international debate on supervisory options," Brash concluded.
